conceptTag: Check a café before you buy it
readerTitle: The café looks profitable. Check what's left after you take over.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (카페 인수, 구독형 앱 인수) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 사업을 살 때는 판매자가 보여주는 숫자가 아니라, 내가 인수한 뒤에도 남는 돈과 은행 계좌로 확인되는 돈으로 값을 매긴다.
misconception: 판매자가 제시한 조정 이익에 업계 평균 배수를 곱하면 적정 인수가가 나온다.

sources.text: 중소기업 인수 실사의 일반 원칙 (조정 이익 검토, 은행 입금과 매출 대조)

factChecks.note: 매출 차이: 장부 매출 $420,000 − 은행·카드 입금 $350,000 = $70,000. 앱 사례: 광고비 $2,000/월, 지원 업무 주 20시간은 가상 수치입니다.
3배 배수는 설명용 가정이며 실제 카페 거래 배수를 제시하는 것이 아닙니다. 카드 문구에서 업계 평균처럼 보이지 않도록 확인하세요.

cards.title: The café looks profitable. Check what's left after you take over.
body: A busy neighborhood café is for sale. The owner wants $240,000.

Her pitch is simple: the café earns $80,000 a year in *adjusted* profit, and three times earnings is a fair price. The tables are full. The coffee is good. Before you sign, two numbers deserve a second look.

image.label: A café for sale with a folder of financial papers on the counter
image.brief: 따뜻한 톤의 동네 카페 카운터. 창문에 "For sale" 안내문, 카운터 위에 서류 폴더와 계산기, 커피잔. 서류 맨 위에 "Adjusted profit $80,000" 문구. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: The profit has been "adjusted." What do you ask first?
body: The tax-year profit is $30,000. The owner adds back $50,000: her own $40,000 salary, a $6,000 "one-time" equipment repair, and $4,000 for her personal car. That's how she gets to $80,000.

options.text: Accept it. Owners always add back their salary
options.feedback: This is **adjusted numbers** at work. Some add-backs are fair, but you'd be paying for $80,000 of profit without checking that any of it survives the change of owner.

options.text: Go line by line: which costs will I still pay after I take over?
options.feedback: This tests each adjustment against your future, not her past. It's the core question behind **adjusted numbers**: does the excluded cost really go away?

options.text: Accept the $80,000 but push the price down to 2.5 times
options.feedback: Negotiating helps, but a lower multiple on the wrong number is still the wrong price. You'd pay $200,000 for a business that may earn far less.

cards.title: Rebuild the profit you'd actually keep.
body: She works behind the counter 60 hours a week. If you don't, you'll pay a manager roughly what she paid herself. The repair happens most years. Only the car truly leaves with her. Real profit: **$34,000**. At three times, that's about $102,000, not $240,000.

cards.title: Adjusted numbers: every add-back is a promise.
body: Each adjustment quietly says, "this cost won't happen again." Your job is to check whether that promise holds for *you*.

Ask three things of every line: Is it really personal or truly one-off? Has it appeared before? Will I pay it, or someone like it, next year? A cost that only moves from the owner's pocket to a manager's paycheck hasn't gone away.

cards.title: The sales records and the bank don't match.
body: The café's sales records show $420,000 last year. Card payments plus bank deposits add up to $350,000. The owner shrugs: the $70,000 gap is cash customers.

options.text: Value the café on $420,000. Cafés take lots of cash
options.feedback: You'd pay for money you can't see. This is **cash and profit disagreeing**: when the books and the bank tell different stories, the books are the easier one to change.

options.text: Value it on the $350,000 you can verify, and ask for proof of the rest
options.feedback: You stay open to the extra sales but don't pay for them until they show up somewhere real. The bank is the anchor when **cash and profit disagree**.

options.text: Walk away. A gap means something's wrong
options.feedback: Caution is healthy, but gaps have innocent causes too. You could lose a good café over a question you never asked.

cards.title: Let the suppliers settle the argument.
body: Sales records are easy to type. Supplier invoices are harder to fake. Beans, milk and cups should roughly match the number of drinks the sales imply.

If the invoices fit $350,000 of sales, the extra $70,000 probably isn't there. Also watch the bank balance over the year. A café that shows a profit while its balance shrinks and supplier bills run late is telling you **cash and profit disagree**.

image.label: Sales ledger, bank statement and supplier invoices side by side
image.brief: 테이블 위에 세 가지 서류를 나란히 배치. 왼쪽 "Sales $420,000" 장부, 가운데 "Bank $350,000" 은행 내역, 오른쪽 원두·우유·컵 납품 송장 묶음. 가운데와 오른쪽을 선으로 연결해 서로 맞는다는 느낌. 실제 은행·브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: A red flag is a question, not a verdict.
body: Some add-backs are honest. A genuine one-off flood repair or a family member on payroll who won't stay are fair to remove.

Gaps can be innocent too: seasonal months, sloppy bookkeeping, a second bank account. The goal is to price what you can confirm, then let the seller prove the rest. For a real purchase, a local accountant or lawyer can run formal checks this lesson doesn't replace.

cards.title: Now it's a small subscription app.
body: A solo founder is selling a scheduling app with $10,000 in monthly recurring revenue and $6,000 in *adjusted* monthly profit. Excluded: $2,000 a month in ads, labeled "growth investment," and the 20 hours a week the founder spends on customer support, unpaid.

options.text: Trust the $6,000. Software margins are high
options.feedback: High margins don't make excluded costs disappear. Monthly ads and support are **adjusted numbers** you'll keep paying.

options.text: Add back the ads and a paid support cost, then compare revenue to the payment processor's payouts
options.feedback: You use both ideas: rebuild the **adjusted numbers**, then check that recurring revenue matches cash that actually arrived.
That confirms the revenue is real, a good start. But real revenue with understated costs still overstates profit.

cards.softwareNote: If users stop seeing ads, new signups may slow and churn may look worse. Ask what revenue looked like in months with less ad spend.

cards.title: Pay for the profit you'll keep and the cash you can see.
body: You used two ideas from this unit. **Adjusted numbers:** test each add-back against life after you take over. **When cash and profit disagree:** let the bank and suppliers check the sales records.
**Try it today:** take your own last year's profit. List anything you'd call "one-time." Did it really happen only once?
